en: The Essential Summary of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, compiled by Master Wonhyo.

Intending to provide an exegesis of this sutra, I shall briefly open six gates for analysis: first, stating the general meaning; second, discerning the core tenets of the sutra; third, clarifying its function of expression; fourth, [explaining... [Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated.]
Title: Five: Subsumption under the Exoteric Teachings; Six: Elucidation of the Textual Meaning.

First, regarding the statement of the general purport: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the great intent of the appearance in the world of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and it is the vast gateway through which the nine realms and four modes of birth are extinguished and entered into the Single Vehicle.

The phrasing is skillful and the meaning profound; there is nothing subtle that it does not exhaustively reach. The expressions are expansive and the principles are serene; there is no Dharma that it does not proclaim.
When the literary expressions are skillfully unfolded, they are like flowers containing fruit;
when the principles are profound and serene, they are like fruit endowed with skillful means (*upāya*).
The profundity of the principle lies in its non-duality and lack of distinction;
the elegance of the phrasing lies in its revelation of the provisional to manifest the real.

To reveal the provisional means that the three carts outside the gate are provisional, the jeweled city along the way is a transformation, the attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree was not the beginning, and the extinction in the grove was not the end.
To reveal the truth means to show that all who are born are my children, and that those of the Two Vehicles shall all become Buddhas;
that their lifespans cannot be measured by calculation, and that the kalpa-fire cannot burn their standing—this is what is called the skillfulness of literary expression.

To speak of "non-duality" means that there is only the single Great Matter; it is because [the Buddha] reveals, shows, awakens, and leads others into his knowledge and vision, which is unsurpassed and non-different, so as to cause them to know and realize it.

To speak of "no distinction" means that the three types are equal: all vehicles and all bodies follow the same principle, for both the mundane world and nirvana are eternally free from the two extremes. This is what is called the profound and subtle nature of the underlying principle.
Thus, its patterns and principles are extinguished and subtle; being nothing other than the profound principle that transcends the coarse, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).
Its provisional splendor unfolds to manifest the reality of the fruit most clearly, and its unsullied beauty is metaphorically likened to the lotus flower.
Yet the wondrous Dharma is sublime and transcendent—what "three" and what "one"?
Reaching back to the most remote antiquity and the profoundest darkness—who is short and who is long?

This [Dharma] is all-encompassing; it is not easy to enter, and for the various disciples to emerge from its vast expanse is truly difficult. Thus, the Tathāgata guides them through skillful means, displaying the coarse body of a human at the Deer Park with the magnificent chariot.
He yoked white oxen at Vulture Peak to manifest infinite longevity.
This is the sublation of one to break through three, and the removal of three to abandon one;
it is the provisional use of the long to transform the short, so that the short ceases and the long is forgotten.

This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; its verbal expressions and characteristics are quiescent. It is vast and without support, solemn and detached from all dependencies. Not knowing how to describe it, one forcibly calls it the "Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma."
Therefore, those who hear [the Dharma] by sharing a seat shall receive the throne of a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra, or a Brahmā;
and those to whose ears even a single phrase reaches shall all obtain the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi.
How much more so, then, can the merit of receiving, upholding, and expounding it be fathomed by thought?
Taking this general significance as the title, it is therefore called the "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra" (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma).
Second, regarding the clarification of the sūtra’s central tenet: this sūtra primarily takes the vast and profound *ekayāna* (One Vehicle) reality-mark (*tathatā*) as its expressed tenet.

Although this is the general statement, to analyze it further, the *ekayāna* reality-mark is briefly said to have two aspects: namely, the person who rides the vehicle (*yātr*) and the vehicle that is ridden (*yātavya*).

The "persons of the One Vehicle" spoken of in this sutra include practitioners of the Three Vehicles, the four types of śrāvakas, and all sentient beings of the three realms born by the four modes of birth; they are all capable of riding the Single Buddha Vehicle, for they are all sons of the Buddha and are all bodhisattvas, as they all possess buddha-nature and shall succeed to the rank of Buddhahood.
Because even sentient beings who lack the nature [for enlightenment] shall all become Buddhas, as stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
"When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they think:

'In all worlds, there are sentient beings of little wisdom, who are foolish, mute, and devoid of the portion of *nirvāṇa*, and who do not give rise to faith—those whom Bodhisattvas might otherwise abandon—I shall tame all such beings, until I sit at the site of enlightenment and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"
"When this mind is generated, the palaces of Māra tremble.
It is further said:
"When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, his manifold vows are fulfilled."
The "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time teach and transform only bodhisattvas.
The "Parable" chapter says:
"Because all sentient beings are my children.
He further said:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction; once a son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future life."
Thus, there is not a single sentient being who is not a child of the Buddha; this is why it is vast.
This realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of nirvāṇa; therefore, it is profoundly deep.
As the treatise states:
"The characteristic of the three realms is that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of nirvāṇa.
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is not separate from the realm of sentient beings, such a person is called one who can ride the Single Buddha Vehicle.
The Dharma mounted by those of the One Vehicle, explained in brief, consists of four aspects:
first, the principle of the One Vehicle and the teaching of the One Vehicle; second, the cause of the One Vehicle and the fruit of the One Vehicle.
The principle of the One Vehicle refers to the single Dharma-realm, which is also called the Dharma-body and the Tathāgatagarbha.
As stated in the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*:
"Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:"
"If there is no differentiation among the three vehicles, for what reason does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of the three vehicles?
The Buddha said:
"When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the three vehicles, they are indicating differences in stages, not differences in vehicles."
This explains the distinctions among persons, not the distinctions among vehicles.

When the Buddhas and Tathāgatas speak of the three vehicles, they do so to show that through small merit one may come to know great merit; yet within the Buddha-dharma, there is no distinction of vehicles.
"Why is this? Because the phenomena of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are without differentiation.
Thus it is said in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"The Dharma-realm is without discrimination; therefore, there are no distinct vehicles.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the three vehicles are taught through differentiation.
Furthermore, this sutra says:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are able to know the ultimate reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of those dharmas.
The commentary explains this, saying: "The 'reality-mark' refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It is the essence of the *dharmakāya*, because its characteristic is unchanging."

Furthermore, the subsequent passage states that they are "the same," which indicates that the nature of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is identical to that of ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, and *pratyekabuddhas*; for the *dharmakāya* is equal and without distinction.
The record states:
The dharmakāya of the Tathāgata and the nature of the tathāgatagarbha are equally possessed by all sentient beings; they are able to transport all beings together back to the original source.
By this principle, there is no distinct vehicle; therefore, this Dharma is taught as having the nature of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is what is called the principle of the Single Vehicle.

As for the teaching of the Single Vehicle: all the verbal instructions spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, from their initial attainment of enlightenment until their parinirvāṇa, without exception lead beings to the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*); for this reason, they are all termed the teaching of the Single Vehicle.
As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter:

"These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable expedients, through various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle."
"Because all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This teaching is universally pervasive throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, being immeasurable and boundless; therefore, it is vast and great.

Therefore, every word and every phrase constitutes the Buddha-vehicle; because it is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, it is profoundly deep. This is what is called the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As for the causes of the One Vehicle, there are generally two:
first, the causal nature (*prakṛtihetu*); second, the causal activity (*kriyāhetu*).
Regarding the "nature as cause": the buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings serves as the cause for the fruit of the three bodies (trikāya).
As stated in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging":
"I do not disparage you; you shall all become buddhas."
The commentary explains this statement:
"Because it demonstrates that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
It further states:
Regarding the two types of śrāvakas—those who are fixed in their destiny and those with overweening pride—the Buddha does not bestow predictions upon them because their faculties are not yet matured;
rather, it is the bodhisattvas who bestow predictions upon them, doing so through skillful means to cause them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.

One should know that based on the intent of this sutra, it is said that those who incline toward tranquility—the two vehicles and sentient beings lacking the [bodhisattva] nature—all possess buddha-nature and shall all become buddhas.

Regarding what is called the "causes for becoming," whether they be noble or ordinary, followers of our own path or external paths, factors conducive to enlightenment (*mārga-bhāga*), or factors conducive to merit (*puṇya-bhāga*), there are no roots of goodness that do not equally lead to unsurpassed bodhi.
As stated in the text below:
"Whether someone prostrates, or merely joins their palms, or even raises a single hand, or slightly bows their head;
if a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and recites 'Namo Buddha' but once, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood."
...and so on, as explained at length.
The *Ben-sheng jing* (Sūtra of the Original Vehicle) states:
"All virtues of both ordinary beings and sages do not receive tainted (*sāsrava*) fruits; they receive only the fruit of eternal abiding."
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:

'If there are those who, being attached to the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence, practice giving or cultivate other roots of goodness within the field of merit of the Buddha, they vow: "May I not enter nirvāṇa in every lifetime."'"
It is impossible that one would not enter parinirvāṇa by means of these roots of goodness.
Although such a person may not seek nirvāṇa with longing, because they have planted various roots of goodness under the Buddha, I declare that this person will certainly enter nirvāṇa.
The *Nigaṇṭhaputra-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the One Vehicle," states:
"The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
'All those in my buddha-field, such as the saṃgha and the Nigaṇṭhaputras, are manifestations through skillful means brought about by the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.'"

These sons of good family from among the various non-Buddhist sects, though they practice the various characteristics of diverse heterodox teachings, all cross over by means of the single bridge of the Buddha-dharma, for there is no other way to cross.
The commentary states:

Based on these passages, one should know that the various virtues of the five vehicles within the Buddha-dharma, as well as the diverse and distinct virtues of the non-Buddhists—all such things as these are the One Vehicle, for they all rely upon the Buddha-nature and possess no different essence.
As the *Dharmapada-śāstra* elucidates this meaning:
"What is meant by 'one who realizes the nature of phenomena'?
It refers to the principle that there is no duality of essence."
"Non-dual essence" means that all immeasurable vehicles are in fact the One Vehicle.

As for the subsequent passage stating, "Those of you who practice the path of the bodhisattva"—referring to those who, having regressed from generating the bodhicitta, generate it again—their previously cultivated roots of goodness do not perish because they will attain the same fruit later. This is said to clarify the supreme meaning of the seed, speaking specifically in terms of the roots of goodness arising from the generation of the mind; it does not mean that other forms of goodness cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, this does not contradict the passage cited previously.

Speaking from this perspective, whether ordinary beings or sages, all sentient beings—whether of the inner path or the outer path—all their roots of goodness emerge from the Buddha-nature and return to the same fundamental source. Such an original state is exhausted only by the Buddhas; for this reason, it is vast and profoundly deep. This is what is called the cause of the One Vehicle.
Regarding the fruit of the One Vehicle, briefly stated, there are two kinds:
namely, the originally existent fruit and the newly arisen fruit.
The originally existent fruit refers to the bodhi of the Dharma-buddha.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Lifespan":

"The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging; there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different."

The commentary states: This passage reveals the essence of the single fruit by means of the single dharma-realm. Because it does not possess a substantial entity, it is not real; because it does not lack a substantial entity, it is not false. Because it is not the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is not "suchness" (tathatā); because it is not the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is not "different."
As stated in the *Mūlayāna-sūtra*:

"The essence of the fruit is perfectly complete; there is no quality that is not fully present and no principle that is not all-pervasive. It is without name and without form; it is not a dharma that can be apprehended, and it is neither an existent entity nor a non-existent entity."
Thus it is said at length.
Furthermore, it states:
"Apart from the two bodies, it exists alone in non-duality. Therefore, this clarifies that the essence of the fruit of the Buddha’s bodhi is the Dharma-Buddha.
Regarding the fruit that first arises, it refers to the other two bodies.
As the treatise states:
"The Bodhi of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha consists in the fulfillment of the practices of the ten stages and the realization of the eternal Nirvāṇa."
As the sutra says:
"Since I truly attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas have passed.
Those who manifest through transformation as Bodhisattvas appear according to what is appropriate for those to be seen.

This refers to his departure from the palace of the Śākyas, his attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree, and the manifestation of the various emanation Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as extensively elucidated in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa.
To summarize: all sentient beings cultivate the myriad practices and equally attain such a fruit of bodhi; this is called the One Vehicle and the fruit of the One Vehicle.
As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter:
"Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself."
"As I vowed in the past, it is now fulfilled; I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way.
According to the commentary:
this passage clearly elucidates that the Tathāgata’s vows have been satisfied.
The reason for this is that they universally transform all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, causing each to attain the Buddha-way according to their needs.
As the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"It is like a bowl of oil; if it is already filled to the brim, even if one more drop is added, it can no longer receive any more."
"When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood and all their vows are fulfilled, it is likewise; not even a single speck of dust's worth of a vow remains unfulfilled.
The *Mahāmegha-guhya-nidhi Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-guhya-nidhi said:"
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of sentient beings of meager merit in future ages, expound such a profound and advanced samādhi as the Tide of the Great Ocean.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, do not speak such words."
Why is this? The appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare, and it is likewise rare for anyone to hear this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*. Why then do you say it is intended only for future beings?
I shall extensively explain its various gateways for the sake of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma; there is nothing throughout the three periods of time that it does not reach.

Based on such passages, one should know that when the Buddhas first attain perfect enlightenment, from the summit of a single thought-moment they universally transform all sentient beings of the three periods of time, so that not a single one fails to achieve unsurpassed bodhi, for their former vows have already been fulfilled.
Suppose there were a person who did not attain enlightenment; this would mean that their former vows would remain unfulfilled.

Although in reality all are delivered and there is no end to them, and although in reality there is no end yet none are left undelivered, it is because they employ the power of infinite wisdom to deliver infinite sentient beings.
Furthermore, the text below this passage in the sutra states:
"The lifespan accomplished by me while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted; it is twice the aforementioned number.
The treatise explains this as follows:

"If I have not yet fulfilled my practice of the bodhisattva path even now, it is because of my original vow; since the realm of sentient beings is not yet exhausted, my vow is not yet consummated, and thus I say it is 'not yet fulfilled. This does not mean that awakening itself is incomplete."

Regarding the statement that "the lifespan thus accomplished again surpasses the aforementioned number," this demonstrates the Tathāgata’s skillful means of eternal life, manifesting a quantity far exceeding the previously mentioned numbers because it cannot be calculated or known.
The intent of this treatise is as follows:

it is to clarify that, because sentient beings of the present have not yet been exhausted, such a time has not arrived where the original vow is fulfilled; it does not mean that while bodhi is already fulfilled, the original vow remains unfulfilled, nor does it mean that while the original vow remains unfulfilled, the Buddha-dharma is already complete.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"As long as all sentient beings have not yet realized bodhi, the Buddha-dharma is not yet sufficient and their original vows are not yet fulfilled.
Therefore, one should know that regarding the vows and bodhi, they are equal when unfulfilled, and equal when fulfilled; this is what is called the fruit of the One Vehicle.

Taken together, these four dharmas—principle and teaching, cause and effect—correspond with one another and collectively transport a single person to *sarvajñā* (omniscience); therefore, these four names are spoken of as the One Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*).

Just as four horses, being mutually responsive, work together to perform a single transport, it is said that the four horses constitute a "single vehicle" (ekayāna); one should know that the principle herein is likewise.
Question:
It may be granted that principle (*nyāya*), teaching (*śāsana*), and cause (*hetu*) together transport sentient beings to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
However, since the fruit (*phala*) has already reached the ultimate state, how can it transport sentient beings in conjunction with these three?
The commentary states:
This involves four meanings.

First, by virtue of the power of the Buddha-fruit existing in the future world, it secretly assists sentient beings, causing them to give rise to wholesome minds; thus, through successive transmission, they are led to the stage of Buddhahood.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Because of the causes and conditions of afflictions in the present life, one may sever the roots of goodness; yet, by virtue of the power and causes and conditions of the Buddha-nature in the future, the roots of goodness will arise once again. Thus it is said.
Second, the Buddha of future fruition manifests various transformations to convert present sentient beings, causing them to attain progress.
As the *Ben-sheng jing* (Sutra of the Original Vehicle) states:
"One personally beholds one's own future fruition, wherein all Buddhas stroke one's head and preach the Dharma; the distinct practices of body and mind are inconceivable. Therefore.
Third, this sutra provides six instances of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), predicting that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they have received these predictions, their minds are inspired to advance toward the cultivation of the future fruit; it is because they belong to that [category] and can be led by it.
The text below states:
"Each son was given one great carriage.

Fourth, this sutra explains that within the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), there is nothing that is not exhausted and no virtue that is not complete; all sentient beings may equally reach this fruit.

Sentient beings, taking these signifiers and signified as their object, give rise to the resolve for enlightenment and advance through the forty stages of mind. They sport with supernatural powers and transform the four classes of birth; therefore, it is said that sentient beings ride upon the vehicle of fruition, and this vehicle of vehicles is able to transport sentient beings of the causal stage.
As the verse states: "At that time, the sons [of the Buddha] were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they mounted these precious chariots and traveled through the four directions.

Because "direction" carries the meaning of "four," one should know that the vehicle of fruition (the *phala-yāna*) operates together with the other three dharmas to convey a single person. When the causes and conditions of these four dharmas harmonize within each individual, they remain free from all extremes and are indestructible. Beyond this, there is nothing further, nor is there anything added. This is called the true characteristic of the vast, profound, and ultimate One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The summarized presentation of the doctrine thus elucidated is as follows.
Third, to clarify the function of the expressive words, the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* states:
"All the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs to this sutra; it opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true reality."
This passage precisely clarifies the superior function of this sutra. There are two kinds of such functions: namely, opening and revealing.
"Opening" refers to opening the gates of the provisional means of the three vehicles; "revealing" refers to revealing the true characteristics of the one vehicle.
Although this is the general explanation, there are three parts within it:
first, the opening; second, the revealing; and third, the combined clarification of the functions of opening and revealing.
First, regarding the meaning of "opening," there are two aspects: namely, the gate that is opened and the function that opens it.
The gates that are opened are precisely the teachings of the Three Vehicles; this is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Briefly, there are four meanings:
first, these are the teachings spoken by the Buddha’s wisdom of expedient means; the name is established based on the *tatpuruṣa* compound, thus it is called the "teachings of expedient means."
Second, it refers to the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which skillfully accord with the capacities of three types of beings;

because these vehicles serve as the means for [attaining] the ultimate, they are termed "teachings of skillful means" (*upāya-deśanā*). Third, they serve as the preliminary skillful means for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) teaching; because the correct teaching of the One Vehicle is subsequently expounded based upon them, they are termed "skillful means" in contrast to that subsequent correct teaching.

Fourth, regarding the principle of the One Vehicle, they are provisionally taught as skillful means rather than as the ultimate truth; this meaning of "skillful means" is termed "skillful means" in contrast to the teaching of ultimate reality. It is based on these four meanings that they are called "skillful means."
This is called a "gate," which has two meanings:
first, the meaning of "exit," because all sons [of the Buddha] rely on this to exit the triple world;
second, the meaning of "entry," because they further rely on this teaching to enter the One Vehicle.
However, a door has two names: if one speaks of it as a "Buddha-door" or a "person-door," then the door is not the Buddha or the person;
if one speaks of it as a "wooden door" or a "bamboo door," then the door is simply wood or bamboo.

Now, the teaching of the three vehicles is called the "gate of skillful means" (upāya-mukha) because it is like a door made of split bamboo; the gate itself is the skillful means, and for this reason it is termed the "gate of skillful means.
Regarding the opening of the gate of skillful means, there are two meanings to "skillful means":
from the perspective of its emergence, when the three vehicles are taught, the gate is opened and not closed.

Anticipating their entry into the ultimate meaning, when the Three Vehicles were taught, [the gate] was closed and not opened; thus, although they had emerged from the three realms, they had not yet entered the One Vehicle. Therefore, the teaching of the One Vehicle is now proclaimed, declaring that the Three Vehicles are merely expedient means, so as to open the gate of expedient means and lead them into the One Vehicle.
As the text below states:
"One should know that by the power of the skillful means of all Buddhas, they distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
These words correctly open the gate of skillful means; all other statements may be understood by this analogy.
Next, the explicit teaching is presented, which also consists of two parts:
first, the object indicated; second, the means of indication. Regarding the true nature of the object indicated:

as previously stated, it refers to the One Vehicle of persons and dharmas, the eternal abiding of the characteristics of dharmas, and the ultimate principle. It cannot be subverted by celestial Māras or non-Buddhists, nor can it be altered by the Buddhas of the three periods of time. For these reasons, it is called the "true nature."
It is neither three nor one; there is no person and no dharma, for nothing at all can be apprehended. Such right contemplation is called the true, ultimate One Vehicle. Why is this so?
Because all that is apprehended is without path and without fruit, neither moving nor emerging; therefore, one knows that, as previously stated, it is not three but is one.
The characteristics of the person who rides and the vehicle ridden do not transcend the four propositions; these constitute "attainment.
How, then, can these be said to be the characteristic of reality? The explanation is as follows:
This statement is not correct.

Why is this so? If one claims that what is not three is one, it does not escape the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). Since such a position involves apprehension (*upalambha*) and is therefore not ultimate, then to hold that "apprehension is wrong and non-apprehension is right" likewise falls within the four propositions; thus, such apprehension is also not right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

If one says that while the expression "non-attainment" is employed as a provisional teaching, one does not grasp at non-attainment according to the literal words—and thus non-attainment does not fall within the four extremes—then others likewise employ the provisional designation of the "One Vehicle," yet do not grasp at the One Vehicle according to the literal words; therefore, the One Vehicle also transcends the four extremes. Consequently, one should know that all such statements are ultimately "neither of these," and must not be grasped according to the literal words.
The two explanations are not different.
Question:
If one does not accept that all words are real, then the teachings of the three vehicles should also be unreal.
Answer:

While the general principle is accepted by all, there is a specific distinction: because the teachings of the Three Vehicles do not contain the three principles at all, whereas the teachings of the One Vehicle do not lack the one principle, the Three Vehicles are provisional and the One Vehicle is the reality.
Although it is not that there is no "one," yet it does not exist as a "one"; therefore, it is also not something that can be attained.
The characteristics of the reality thus revealed are as follows.
There are two kinds of functional manifestations that can be revealed:

First, it is revealed and shown: just as when the three [vehicles] were previously opened as a skillful means, one immediately knew that the One Vehicle is the reality; it is like seeing the objects within upon opening a door.

Second is the teaching of a distinct opening, which differs from the previous opening of the three vehicles by separately expounding the One Vehicle; because upon hearing it, one attains enlightenment regarding the meaning of the One Vehicle, it is like using one's hand to open [a box] so that the objects within can be seen.
As it is said in the text:
"The Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
Such statements as these demonstrate the true nature.
Third, regarding the combined clarification of the function (*vṛtti*), there are four meanings within this single clarification:
first, taking the preceding three as a single function, because the teachings of the three vehicles are themselves the teaching of the One Vehicle.
Second, it leads the three to reach the one, because it causes those of the three vehicles to equally attain the fruit of the One Vehicle.
Third, it unifies the three and returns them to the one, because it brings back the previously taught causes and fruits of the three vehicles to the fundamental principle of the One Vehicle.

Fourth, it "destroys three and establishes one," because it refutes the attachment to the distinct destinies of the three vehicles to establish the principle that they all ultimately converge in the One Vehicle.
This sutra possesses these four kinds of superior functions; therefore, it is said to "open the gate of skillful means and reveal the true reality."
Question:
Regarding "using the three as one" and "bringing the three to one," what serves as the proof for these two?
Answer:
The "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"The Buddha expounds all dharmas through innumerable expedient means; these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
This passage is precisely the proof that the three vehicles are used as one.
Furthermore, it is said:
"All these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes.
These words are precisely the proof that the three vehicles lead to the one vehicle.
Question:
Regarding the convergence of the three causes and effects back into the single fundamental reality, does this mean that all three are non-real and thus return to the one reality?
Or does it mean that only two are non-real and thus return to the one reality?
If it were as in the latter case, why does the Sūtra say:
"I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the Dharma of the three vehicles"?
If it were as in the former case, why does it further say:
"Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real.
Answer: Some may say that all three are unreal, as stated in the preceding text.

Regarding the statement that "one is real while two are not true": among the three [vehicles], the one that is identical to the single vehicle (the Buddha-vehicle) and the one where there are no three vehicles are both the Buddha-vehicle; they are collectively described as "real.
The remaining two do not require further opening [of their provisional nature], and thus are specifically said to be "not real."
For this reason, the two passages do not contradict one another.
Some may say that only the two [vehicles] are not real, as stated in the subsequent passage.
As for the statement that all three vehicles are expedient means, it is because two non-realities are added to the one reality and spoken of together as three; thus, these three are not real.
It is like a person who actually has one fruit in their hand, yet uses skillful means to speak of three.
These three are not real, because there are no three fruits; however, when examined and analyzed, one fruit is real while two are skillful means, because that one fruit does exist.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The single Buddha Vehicle is opened into three parts.

This is like a person dividing one *dou* of rice into three heaps; one may say "the three heaps are brought back to one," or one may say "the two heaps are brought back [to one]. Bringing the three together and bringing the two together are identical in meaning and do not contradict one another.
Some may say that the two preceding passages each have a distinct meaning and cannot be harmonized as one.
The reason for this is that the teachings of the Three Vehicles are of two kinds:
first, the Separate Teaching (biejiao); second, the Common Teaching (tongjiao).

In the Separate Teaching (*prātibhedika*), the three vehicles are all unreal and are merely skillful means (*upāya*). This is because that teaching states that for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* one cultivates only the four perfections (*pāramitā*), during the hundred eons one cultivates the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and in one's final existence one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, attaining unexcelled enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree through such causes and conditions constitutes the Buddha-vehicle; therefore, even the Buddha-vehicle is a skillful means.

If we discuss the three vehicles as taught in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Buddha-vehicle is the reality, while the other two are certainly not true. This is because that teaching states that by fully practicing the six perfections and myriad deeds throughout the ten stages, one attains *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); this fruit of *sarvajñā* does not conjoin with the three periods of time. Such a cause and effect is ultimately real; this is the Buddha-vehicle—how could it be a mere expedient?
Therefore, one should know that the meanings of these two passages differ.

The statement, "I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the three vehicles," refers to the three vehicles as taught in the distinct teaching (biejiao). The statement, "There is only this one reality; the other two are not true," refers to the three vehicles as taught in the common teaching (tongjiao); all other passages should be understood in this same way.
Question:
If it is said that the causes and effects of the three vehicles according to the distinct teaching (biejiao) are all expedient means and thus converge into one,
does this convergence refer to a single cause or a single fruit?
Answer:
Within the single Buddha-vehicle, three are taught through differentiation; therefore, according to their original inclinations toward either cause or fruit, what is the meaning of this?
Whether it be the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, whether cause or fruit, both are differentiated into two within the single cause.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is all the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
One should know that these two both return to a single cause; because they return to a single cause, they ultimately result in a single fruit.
In that teaching, it is said: "The differentiation of the causes and fruits of the Buddha-vehicle [reveals] a small portion of the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha-ground.
As the sutra states:
"Since I truly attained Buddhahood, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed."
One should know that what they teach regarding the causes and effects of the Buddha-vehicle all ultimately converge within the fruit of this single vehicle.

If there are bodhisattvas who, relying on those teachings, resolve to practice by taking the Buddha beneath the tree as their object, such vows and practices converge upon a single cause, for they are identical to the two vehicles in not yet having reached the final fruit.
Speaking generally, one should formulate four propositions:
first, attributing the causes of skillful means to the cause of ultimate reality, namely the causes of bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles;
second, attributing the fruits of skillful means to the fruit of ultimate reality, namely the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment beneath the tree.
Third, returning the cause of skillful means to the fruit of ultimate reality, which refers to the bodhisattva practice before the Buddha under the tree;
fourth, returning the fruit of skillful means to the cause of ultimate reality, which refers to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of those of the two vehicles.
These four propositions are summarized in order to explain the convergence of the three vehicles into one.
Question:
Within the teachings of skillful means, there are the vehicles of humans and devas; for what reason are these two not converged, while only those three are converged?
Answer:
The phrase "convergence of the three" also subsumes these two.
The reason for this is that within the teachings of the Lotus Sūtra, it is stated that there are two types of the Three Vehicles:
The first refers to the parable of the three carts, which appears in the "Parable Chapter";
the second refers to the parable of the three types of grass, which appears in the "Herbs Chapter.
What is the meaning of this?
The two vehicles of humans and devas combined are termed the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), like small medicinal herbs.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are termed the Middle Vehicle (*madhyamayāna*), like medium medicinal herbs.
Bodhisattvas who resolve their minds according to that distinct teaching are said to be of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), like great medicinal herbs.

These three vehicles encompass the five vehicles; however, while those humans and devas meet with the cause, they do not meet with the fruit, for the fruit is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and does not constitute a single cause.
That cause of wholesome dharmas possesses two functions; however, the function of the retributive cause is not included here because its fruition is exhausted.
The function of the outflowing cause is what is intended here, because its fruition is never exhausted.
By understanding this meaning of the cause, one enters the first proposition.
Question:
While the principle of synthesizing the three into one has already been clarified, how can it be known that the three are refuted and the one is established?
Answer:
To understand this meaning, there are both extensive and concise explanations.
To speak briefly, it involves refuting four kinds of triads:

First, the insistence that the three teachings are definitively not expedient means; second, the insistence that the three types of persons are definitively distinct destinies; third, the insistence that the three causes produce separate results; and fourth, the insistence that the three fruits have separate ultimate limits.

By shattering these four kinds of grasped characteristics and dispelling the four kinds of grasping views, one establishes the reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Specifically, by establishing the One Teaching, the three teachings are shattered; by establishing the One Person, the three persons are shattered; by establishing the One Cause, the three causes are shattered; by establishing the One Fruit, the three fruits are shattered; and by establishing the One Rational Nature, all four sets of three are comprehensively shattered.
Because the four "ones" are all identical in principle to the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), they are explained briefly in this manner.

To discuss them extensively, seven similes and three types of equality are taught in order to refute the ten kinds of attachments held by ordinary beings and sages; the meaning of this will be explained in the sixth section.
The third section concludes the explanation of the function of the title.

Fourth, regarding the interpretation of the title: to preserve the original Sanskrit phonetics, it should be called *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*, which in Chinese is translated as the *Sutra of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma*.
Regarding the term "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma), there are briefly four meanings:
first, skillfulness; second, excellence; third, subtlety; and fourth, transcendence.

Regarding the term "skillful" (*kauśalya*): this sutra skillfully opens the gate of expedient means (*upāya*), skillfully extinguishes the views of clinging to the three [vehicles], skillfully reveals the mark of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), and skillfully engenders the wisdom of oneness; because it serves as the true guide through these four meanings, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*).

Regarding the term "supremely sublime": this sutra is able to proclaim all Buddha-dharmas, demonstrate all spiritual powers, reveal all secret treasuries, and expound all profound matters. Because it is supremely sublime by virtue of these four meanings, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).
As stated in the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers":

"To state it briefly, all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, all the sovereign supernatural powers of the Tathāgata, all the secret treasuries of the Tathāgata, and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are proclaimed, revealed, and expounded within this sutra."
Therefore, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*).

Regarding the term "subtle and wondrous": the fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) taught in this sutra is such that there is no sublime virtue that is not perfected, no defilement that is not purified, no principle that is not exhaustive, and no world that is not delivered; for these four reasons, it is named the "Subtle and Wondrous Dharma."
As stated in the "Parable Chapter":
"This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, the foremost in purity; it transcends all worlds and is unsurpassed.
Therefore, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).

Regarding the term "absolutely marvelous": the dharma-characteristics of the One Vehicle taught in this sutra are vast, profound, beyond words, and transcending thought; for these four reasons, it is called the absolutely marvelous Dharma.
As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter:
"This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; its words and signs are quiescent. Among all other classes of sentient beings, there is none who can understand it."
Therefore, among these four meanings, the skillful and sublime Dharma establishes the name through its function as the signifier;
the subtle and peerless meaning derives its designation from the doctrine it signifies.

Taken together, it fully encompasses these sixteen kinds of skillful, supreme, subtle, and transcendent, most wondrous meanings—the non-dual path of the ten directions and the three periods of time. For this reason, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma).
The brief explanation of the name "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*) is thus.
Regarding the metaphor of the lotus, there are both specific and general applications. As for the general application:

this flower necessarily consists of the integration of four parts—the petals, the filaments, the calyx, and the fruit—and is exceptionally beautiful and exquisite. This serves as a metaphor for how this sutra integrates four sublime meanings to form a single scripture; therefore, it is named the "Sublime Dharma."
To explain this in detail, there are four meanings:

First, among the four varieties of lotus, the *pundarīka* is the white lotus; it is pure white and distinct, with its petals fully opened and its core clearly revealed. This serves as a metaphor for this sutra, which is skillfully clear and distinct in its opening of the provisional and revealing of the real.

Second, this flower has three names: when it has not yet blossomed, it is called *kumuda*; when it is about to fall, it is called *kamala*; and when it is fully blossomed but not yet withered—during its period of peak splendor—it is termed *puṇḍarīka*. This serves as a metaphor for this sutra, representing the excellence of its proclamation and exposition during the time when the great capacity [of sentient beings] is fully awakened.

Third, these flowers not only emerge from the mud and water, but are also perfectly fragrant and pure, endowed with every excellence; this serves as a metaphor for the subtle and wondrous nature of the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna) taught in this sutra, which emerges from the turbidity of afflictions, leaves the ocean of birth and death, and is perfected with all virtues.

Fourth, these flowers not only possess broad petals and deep calyxes, but they also do not cling to drops of water nor are they stained by dust or grime; this serves as a metaphor for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) taught in this sutra—its Dharma-gate is vast, its principles are profound, and it is the most exquisite state that transcends words and cuts off all conceptual thought.
Because these four meanings share commonalities with the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*), this metaphor is employed to establish the title of the work.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the category of teaching: under which teaching is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* subsumed?
Is this of definitive meaning (nītārtha),
or is it of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha)?
Some say that this sutra is of non-definitive meaning.
The reason for this is that, broadly speaking, the Buddha's teachings comprise three wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*):

first, the wheel of Dharma with signs (*sanimitta-dharmacakra*), which is turned solely for those setting out on the Śrāvaka vehicle by relying upon the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, as found in the *Āgama* sūtras and similar texts.

The second is the wheel of dharma without signs (*animitta-dharmacakra*), which is turned solely for those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle, because it turns the wheel of dharma based on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); as in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others.

Third is the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma of signlessness, which is turned for the sake of those who have set out upon all three vehicles, based on the emptiness of all phenomena and their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*);
it is unsurpassed and admits of no further superior, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other such texts.
Among these, the first two are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), while the third wheel of Dharma is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This point is explained in detail in that treatise.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* belongs to the second category, as the verse states:
"All dharmas from the very beginning are eternally characterized by quiescence; when the sons of the Buddha have practiced the path, they shall become Buddhas in a future age. Thus it is said.
Therefore, one should know that this is subsumed under the second wheel of Dharma, which is signless (animitta).
Since it belongs to the second [wheel], it is of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
This point is proven by two passages of scripture:
First, as stated in that same *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*:

"A person belonging to the lineage of a śrāvaka who is solely intent upon tranquility cannot, even if they receive from all Buddhas various skillful means of transformation through courageous applications, ever be made to sit at the site of enlightenment and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."

Why is this? Because they have, from the very beginning, only an inferior spiritual disposition; because their compassion is consistently weak; and because they are consistently terrified by all forms of suffering.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Second, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Regarding the intention of sentient beings who delight in happiness: for example, in order to cause those of indeterminate lineage to abandon their inferior intentions, it is prophesied that great śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood."
Furthermore, it is said that there is but one vehicle, and no second.
According to this,
since that sūtra is a definitive teaching of ultimate reality, it states that śrāvakas will never attain Buddhahood.
Thus we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s statement that all śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood is a skillful means (*upāya*) and an incomplete teaching (*neyārtha*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharma* states:
"This was spoken in accordance with the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings; it is not a direct exposition of the true principle."
The Sūtras excel in their literary expression, while the Abhidharma excels in its logical reasoning.
Because there is such dual evidence, one should know that the teaching of the *Dharmapuṣpa* on the One Vehicle is certainly not a definitive teaching of ultimate meaning (*nītārtha*).
Some may say that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the ultimate definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Why is this so?
Because all the teachings expounded by the Tathāgata throughout his entire career can be briefly subsumed into no more than three wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
What are the three?
First is the Dharma-wheel of the Root; second is the Dharma-wheel of the Branches and Extremities; third is the Dharma-wheel of Gathering the Extremities Back to the Root.

As for the Dharma-wheel of the Root, it refers to when the Buddha, immediately after attaining enlightenment, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, extensively expounded for the Bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of a single cause and a single fruit; this is the teaching of the Root.

However, those of meager merit and dull faculties are utterly unable to hear of a single cause and a single fruit; therefore, within the One Buddha Vehicle, I have differentiated and taught three vehicles—this is what is called the teaching of the branches and the secondary.

For over forty years, he taught the doctrine of the Three Vehicles to refine and temper their minds; now, at this assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, they have finally attained the convergence of the three into one—this is precisely the teaching of subsuming the branches back into the root.

As clarified in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," the elder sitting upon the lion throne, surrounded by his retinue and displaying various precious objects, refers precisely to the fundamental teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Because he could not call his son back, he secretly dispatched two men who stripped off their precious and noble robes and donned tattered, soiled garments; this is what is meant by "hiding one while explaining three," which constitutes the teaching of the provisional branches.

Just as a wealthy elder, knowing that [his children] are all of inferior capacity, first subdues their minds and then teaches them great wisdom—this refers to the teaching of "gathering the branches back to the root.
This is evidenced by textual passages throughout various sections; one should know that herein, the first and last teachings are both the ultimate, definitive exposition (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the second teaching, the exposition of three within one is entirely a provisional teaching of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*).
To establish this point, there are two types of clear evidence:
first, the Sūtras; second, the Abhidharma.
Regarding the *sūtras*, I shall briefly cite three passages. First, as stated in the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct":
"This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."

The entire world is full of enmity and difficult to trust; that which was not previously spoken is now being spoken. This is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas, the most profound among all teachings, granted at the very end—just as a powerful king, having long guarded a bright jewel, finally bestows it upon others.
Second, the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter states:
"These are the skillful means of all Buddhas; they distinguish and teach the three vehicles, yet there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, and it is for the sake of resting that they speak of two."
Third, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"Arhats and pratyekabuddhas, having reached the ultimate consummation of the four knowledges and attained the place of rest, are also Tathāgatas."
These are teachings given through skillful means that are incomplete and of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Passages such as these cannot be cited in their entirety.
Regarding the Abhidharma, I shall briefly cite texts from three locations.

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "Because the two types of śrāvakas—the definitive and those with overweening pride—have not yet matured their faculties, the Buddha does not bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment; rather, it is the bodhisattvas who bestow the prediction."
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s bestowing of predictions: it is because he employs skillful means to cause [beings] to resolve their minds [on enlightenment].
Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Question:"
"Since the body received by an Arhat through the causal conditions of previous lives must necessarily be extinguished, in what place does he abide to fulfill the Buddha-way?
He replied:
"When one attains Arhatship, because the causes and conditions of the outflows (āsrava) within the three realms are exhausted, one is no longer reborn within the three realms."

There is a Pure Buddha who has emerged from the triple world; even the name of affliction does not exist there. In that land, one establishes oneself before the Buddha and hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, thereby perfecting the path to Buddhahood.
Third, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Question:
Regarding the statement that icchantikas lack the nature for nirvāṇa and thus never enter nirvāṇa, what is the meaning of this?"
This is for the purpose of demonstrating and revealing the causes for slandering the Mahāyāna.
What meaning does this clarify? It means:

"This was said for the purpose of turning back the mind that slanders the Mahāyāna and the mind that does not seek the Mahāyāna; it was spoken based on immeasurable time, because they truly possess the nature of purity."

Based on such passages, one should understand that the various teachings which state that there are two vehicles who definitely do not attain Buddhahood, as well as the statements regarding sentient beings without the Buddha-nature (*agotra*), are all expedient means and teachings of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*).
If it is said that "there is but one vehicle and no second, and all sentient beings shall become Buddhas," such a sūtra is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Question:
If the position of the first master is established, how should one reconcile the scriptural passages cited by the latter master?
That master replied:
"All the various passages taught in the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teachings are intended to protect those of indeterminate nature; they are all skillful means."
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

The text of the *Dharmapada-śāstra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* also describe the intent of the subsequent provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*). As for the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* stating that "Arhats are born in the Pure Land," this refers to Śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
By this reasoning, there is likewise no contradiction.
Question:
If the position of the latter master is established, how can the proofs cited previously be reconciled?
That master explains:

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states, "They can never be made to sit at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. This clarifies that they are destined to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); it means one can never prevent them from entering that state of no-remainder, as they will directly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening [only after doing so]. Therefore, they are said to be "exclusively oriented toward tranquility" (*ekānta-śama-yāyin*).

However, when those śrāvakas enter the state of nirvana without remainder, they remain for eighty thousand kalpas, or sixty thousand, forty thousand, or twenty thousand; thereafter, they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and immediately enter the Great Vehicle, being born in a pure land where they fully perfect the Buddha-way.

As for those of indeterminate lineage, they enter the Great [Vehicle] while abiding solely on the stage of having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), because this is clearly stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Therefore, that sūtra is likewise not contradictory.

The statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* that the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is a skillful means (*upāya*) expresses the intention behind the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), rather than being a discourse on ultimate reality. This is as those who adhere to the Three Vehicles say:

"The fifteen [factors] that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)"—this is spoken in reference to coarse characteristics and objective spheres, and is not the ultimate, true principle.
Therefore, one should know that the Abhidharma treatises may sometimes recount the texts of the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*);
by this principle, there is no contradiction.
Question:
The two masters’ interpretations are mutually contradictory; which one is the reality, and which one is superior?
Answer:
All of these are from the sūtras and śāstras; how could they be anything but true?
The reason for this is that to protect the minds of those whose disposition is exclusively directed toward tranquility (śama), one takes what the former master transmits as true;

to protect the minds of those with indeterminate lineage (aniyata-gotra), one takes what the latter master explains as true. This is because each brings harmony and resolution according to the specific capacities of sentient beings.

If one were to judge their respective merits and shortcomings based on reason, that teacher’s doctrine is narrow and shallow; for he asserts that the Buddha-nature does not pervade all things, and he further claims that the two [natures] are ultimately subject to annihilation.

The meaning of the second master is broad and extensive, whereas the former [position] is narrow and brief; this can be understood through their respective meanings. Thus, to interpret a broad and extensive text with a narrow and brief meaning results in a text that is difficult to comprehend.
Conversely, to accommodate a narrow and brief text with a broad and extensive meaning, the brevity of the text is not a flaw, and the meaning becomes easy to understand.
Based on this reasoning, the latter teaching is declared to be superior.
Therefore, one should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the ultimate teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, by relying on this principle to interpret all textual passages, those passages that appear contradictory can all be successfully reconciled.
This is because within the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) of the ultimate doctrine, there are not a few expedient expressions that are not definitive; as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*:
"All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas equally share this single, wondrous, pure path; they are all equally identical in this single, ultimate, pure suchness (*tathatā*)."
"This principle constitutes the core tenet of that sūtra.
Therefore, that sūtra is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

However, when that sūtra states, "Śrāvakas who have entered into tranquility can never attain sitting at the site of enlightenment," such passages are taught as skillful means (*upāya*). This was a teaching of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) formulated as a skillful means in order to protect the minds of those fixed in the two vehicles.
By this principle, the statement that "the nature of all phenomena is equal" is explained as being of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Thus, these two passages do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, within this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said: "For the sake of [providing] rest, he manifests a jeweled city; having allowed them to rest there for a while, he ultimately leads them to the fruit of Buddhahood."
Based on this principle, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught; this constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the sūtra.

This sūtra also contains words of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*): it states directly, "There is only [the One Vehicle], neither two nor three. This passage does not definitively state that there are no practices of the two vehicles of those seeking tranquility (*śamaikayānika*); in reality, the practices of the two vehicles of those seeking tranquility do exist. Therefore, the statement that they do not exist is a skillful means (*upāya*).
For this reason, there is also a logical basis for the *Abhidharma* treatises to describe [this] as a skillful means (*upāya*).
This was transmitted on the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the sixth year of Kōan.
